newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU finance ministers to focus on TENs, not EMU.
newsitem.headline: EU finance ministers to focus on TENs, not EMU.

text.p: European Commission President Jacques Santer's long and tortured battle to secure more money for trans-European road and rail links, is expected to come to a bitter end when EU finance ministers meet on Monday.

Santer's proposal to earmark a further 1.0 billion Ecus ($1.3 billion) for the so-called TENs projects (trans-European networks), has consistently fallen on deaf ears, with many governments insistent that the money go towards reducing national budget deficits.

With nearly all of the EU's 15 nations engaged in an all-out sprint to meet the Maastricht treaty's tough criteria on budgets and debt for monetary union, EU spending proposals which are considered less than urgent have received scant support.
The road and rail networks were an integral part of Santer's confidence pact for employment, an initiative launched earlier in the year to tackle the union's mounting jobless rate.

The 14 priority projects, indentified by EU leaders at a summit in Essen in December 1994, include high-speed trains between Paris and Cologne and between Frankfurt and London, plus motorways in Greece, Spain and Portugal.
EU finance ministers, who gather in Luxembourg on Monday, are not expected to talk about economic and monetary union (EMU), officials said.
"EMU is not on the agenda," said a Commission official, adding, that the next critical ministerial meeting on the single currency would come in early November.
At a meeting of the EU's monetary committee this week, little progress was made on finalising a plan to curb budget deficits among countries forming a common currency in 1999.
Debate over the so-called budget stability pact centres on a precise definition of the extraordinary economic circumstances which would let a government avoid punitive sanctions.

All are agreed that a country which runs an excessive deficit inside EMU -- defined as over three percent of total output -- should face fines of an appropriate size. But here again, there is debate over size of the penalty.
The meeting also comes amid a backdrop of heightened speculation over Finland's and Italy's near-term entry into Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM).
Finland, in particular, is seen joining the ERM relatively soon, given ongoing attempts by the Finnish central bank to limit the markka's appreciation.
EU monetary officials, meanwhile, say Italy's return to the currency grid is likely to come a bit later in the year given the diversity of opinion over what the appropriate entry rate should be.
France has often argued for the lira to strengthen further before the EU lets the lira back in. Both the lira and sterling left the ERM in September 1992 after a severe currency crisis.

Although market speculation of a decision on either the markka or lira at Monday's meeting is likely to intensify, officials say such matters are more likely to be decided among the EU's monetary committee over a weekend.
